title: Two Unitree G1 humanoid flaws enable root RCE, one over Bluetooth
subtitle: Researcher Andreas Makris (Boschko) disclosed a wormable BLE bug — CVE-2026-76640, dubbed UniBLEed — that lets an attacker within Bluetooth range take root control of any Unitree G1 EDU humanoid without pairing.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Security researcher Andreas Makris (Boschko) published details of two vulnerabilities in Unitree's G1 EDU humanoid robot on August 27 that each allow unauthenticated remote code execution as root. The first, CVE-2026-76640, has been named UniBLEed: it uses a Bluetooth Low Energy write path that accepts a bootstrap interaction without pairing, then triggers a buffer overflow during Wi-Fi provisioning to execute arbitrary code as root on the robot's locomotion PC. The second, CVE-2026-76639, uses a path-traversal in the chat_go daemon to reach bashrunner and execute root code. UniBLEed is wormable — a compromised G1 can spread the same exploit to any other G1 in Bluetooth range.

The wormable property is what raises this above a normal disclosure. BLE-based propagation means a single compromised humanoid on a factory floor, in a lab, or in a demonstration space can silently root every other G1 in a ~10-meter radius, without pairing, without user interaction, and without needing network connectivity of its own. Unitree patched the cloud account-to-robot ownership check in July, which closed one link in the attack chain, but the BLE bootstrap flaw remained until this disclosure. Boschko released the write-up only after coordinated disclosure with the vendor.

The context is that humanoid deployments have quietly shifted from lab curiosities to enterprise procurement. Unitree completed its Shanghai IPO earlier in August at a $904M raise; XPeng's Iron and Figure's newest platforms are all reaching customers; and industrial buyers are placing multi-unit orders for warehousing, security, and manufacturing pilots. A wormable root-RCE class of vulnerability in that fleet is materially different from the same bug class in a phone — a compromised humanoid has actuators, cameras, microphones, and the ability to physically move.

Takeaway for learners: when you evaluate any embodied-AI product, ask three questions the researcher's write-up demonstrates matter — what wireless interfaces are exposed before authentication, what can code running as root actually cause the robot to do, and how does the vendor push patches to fielded units. The AI reasoning stack riding on top is not the interesting attack surface here; the boring provisioning code underneath is.
